stem: Which observation in Sjögren's disease most strongly suggests a contribution from sex hormones to pathogenesis?
choices: A. Predominance in XX individuals at a 15–20:1 ratio with onset >50 years
B. Strong association with class II MHC alleles across genome-wide studies
C. Earlier age of onset in childhood-onset disease relative to adult disease
D. Higher disease prevalence in second-degree relatives of male probands
E. Reduced incidence in women on long-term oral contraceptive therapy
explanation: Sjögren's shows striking female predominance (15–20:1) with onset typically after age 50 → strongly implicates a sex-hormone contribution. The XX bias is independent of (and additive to) the MHC genetic association.

wrongExplanations.1: MHC association is real and is the most robust GENETIC association, but it does not by itself implicate hormones.
wrongExplanations.2: Childhood-onset Sjögren's is uncommon. Onset is typically >50 years, not earlier in pediatric forms.
wrongExplanations.3: Familial clustering through male relatives is not a documented feature; the disease overwhelmingly affects females.
wrongExplanations.4: Oral contraceptive effects on incidence are not established in the lecture and would not be the primary line of evidence.

eli5: Almost everyone who gets Sjögren's is female (about 15–20 women for every 1 man), and it usually shows up after 50. That huge gender gap is the clue that hormones probably play a role.

stem: Of the autoantibody tests in Sjögren's disease, which has the highest patient detection rate?
choices: A. Anti-Ro/SSA, detected in roughly 60–80% of patients with sicca features
B. Anti-La/SSB, found in 60–80% of patients and often co-positive with anti-Ro/SSA
C. Anti-muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antibodies targeting acinar gland tissue
D. Antinuclear antibodies, found in approximately 90% of Sjögren's patients
E. High-titer rheumatoid factor, identified in roughly 75% of all Sjögren's cases
explanation: ANA is positive in ~90% of Sjögren's patients → highest detection rate of any antibody in the panel. Anti-Ro/SSA = 60–80%, anti-La/SSB = 60–80%, RF = 75%. ANA is sensitive but not specific.

wrongExplanations.1: Anti-Ro/SSA is highly suggestive but lower prevalence (~60–80%) than ANA.
wrongExplanations.2: Anti-La/SSB is in the same 60–80% range and almost always co-occurs with anti-Ro/SSA, but is not the most prevalent.
wrongExplanations.3: Anti-muscarinic ACh receptor antibodies are mechanistically informative for xerostomia but are not the highest-prevalence serology.
wrongExplanations.4: RF is found in ~75% of patients — high, but ANA at ~90% is higher.

eli5: Almost every Sjögren's patient (90%) tests positive for antinuclear antibodies, but lots of other diseases do too. So ANA is sensitive but not specific.

stem: Which slit-lamp ophthalmic stain is used specifically to evaluate the conjunctiva rather than the cornea?
choices: A. Fluorescein, used principally for measuring tear break-up time and corneal damage staining
B. Rose Bengal stain, applied to mark damaged cornea and conjunctival epithelium broadly
C. Methylene blue, traditionally applied for pH-dependent staining of acidic surfaces and cells
D. Trypan blue, used to mark non-viable cells in cell-culture experiments and assays routinely
E. Lissamine green, used for selective conjunctival staining in slit-lamp examination broadly
explanation: Lissamine green stains damaged conjunctival epithelium specifically. The slit-lamp panel for Sjögren's: Rose Bengal (cornea AND conjunctiva), Fluorescein (tear break-up time, corneal staining), Lissamine green (conjunctiva).

wrongExplanations.1: Fluorescein is for tear break-up time and corneal staining, not specifically the conjunctiva.
wrongExplanations.2: Rose Bengal stains damaged epithelium of BOTH cornea and conjunctiva — not conjunctiva-specific.
wrongExplanations.3: Methylene blue is not part of the Sjögren's slit-lamp panel.
wrongExplanations.4: Trypan blue is a cell-culture viability stain, not part of clinical slit-lamp evaluation.

eli5: Three stains, three jobs. Rose Bengal stains cornea AND conjunctiva. Fluorescein stains tear film and cornea. Lissamine green is the one that's just for the conjunctiva.

stem: What is the diagnostic finding on minor salivary gland biopsy in Sjögren's disease?
choices: A. Caseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells in the gland stroma broadly
B. Dense lymphocytic infiltration of glandular tissue with gland destruction broadly
C. Diffuse plasma cell infiltrate with storiform fibrosis on H&E section microscopy
D. Periductal acid-fast bacilli with chronic inflammation in fibrotic glandular tissue
E. Eosinophil-rich inflammation with reactive lymphoid hyperplasia in scattered foci
explanation: Salivary gland biopsy in Sjögren's shows dense lymphocytic infiltration with destruction of glandular tissue → focal lymphocytic sialadenitis. This is the histologic gold standard supporting the diagnosis.

wrongExplanations.1: Caseating granulomas with giant cells suggest tuberculosis or other infectious granulomatous disease, not Sjögren's.
wrongExplanations.2: Storiform fibrosis with IgG4+ plasma cells defines IgG4-related disease — a key Sjögren's mimic but not Sjögren's itself.
wrongExplanations.3: Periductal acid-fast bacilli describe mycobacterial infection (e.g., parotid TB), not Sjögren's.
wrongExplanations.4: Eosinophil-rich infiltrate suggests allergic/parasitic processes, not Sjögren's.

eli5: If a doctor takes a tiny piece of your inner-lip salivary gland and sees it packed with lymphocytes that have wrecked the gland, that's the picture of Sjögren's.

stem: Which test objectively quantifies saliva production as part of Sjögren's evaluation?
choices: A. Rose Bengal staining of the buccal mucosa under slit-lamp magnification examination
B. Schirmer's test using filter paper placed in the lower conjunctival sac for 5 minutes
C. Whole (whole-mouth) sialometry, which measures total saliva output over a timed period
D. Salivary scintigraphy with technetium-99m showing tracer uptake and excretion patterns
E. Submandibular gland ultrasound with elastography of the glandular parenchymal tissue
explanation: Whole sialometry measures saliva production directly → quantifies the functional consequence of glandular destruction. It complements antibody serology and Schirmer's testing in the diagnostic workup.

wrongExplanations.1: Rose Bengal is an ophthalmic stain for the EYE, not a saliva test.
wrongExplanations.2: Schirmer's test measures TEAR production, not saliva.
wrongExplanations.3: Salivary scintigraphy can be supportive imaging but is not the lecture's named saliva-quantification test.
wrongExplanations.4: Ultrasound/MRI is mentioned for imaging but does not directly quantify saliva output.

eli5: Sialometry is just a fancy word for measuring how much spit you make. Doctors collect it for a few minutes and weigh it.

stem: A Sjögren's patient has residual functional acinar tissue on biopsy yet still has severe xerostomia. Which autoantibody best explains this paradox?
choices: A. Anti-Ro/SSA, by inducing complement-mediated destruction of acinar cells progressively over time
B. Anti-La/SSB, by interfering with intracellular RNA stability in salivary epithelial cells locally
C. Antinuclear antibodies, by binding nuclear antigens and triggering inflammatory cascades broadly
D. Anti-muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antibodies blocking the parasympathetic gland stimulation
E. Rheumatoid factor, by activating Fc receptors on infiltrating effector cells locally in glands
explanation: Anti-muscarinic ACh receptor antibodies → block parasympathetic M3 receptor signaling on acinar cells → even surviving glands cannot be stimulated to secrete saliva → functional xerostomia despite preserved tissue. This explains residual symptoms even when destruction is incomplete.

wrongExplanations.1: Anti-Ro/SSA contributes to gland inflammation but does not explain dysfunction in residual tissue specifically.
wrongExplanations.2: Anti-La/SSB binds RNA transcripts but is a marker, not a functional blocker of secretion in surviving glands.
wrongExplanations.3: ANA is a sensitive but mechanistically nonspecific marker — not the explanation for blocked stimulation.
wrongExplanations.4: RF is a marker of B cell hyperactivity, not an inhibitor of secretory function.

eli5: Spit glands need a 'go' signal from nerves through muscarinic receptors. These antibodies plug those receptors, so even healthy glands can't be told to make spit.

stem: A 60-year-old presents with bilateral salivary and lacrimal gland enlargement, sicca symptoms, and elevated serum IgG4. Histology shows storiform fibrosis with IgG4-positive plasma cells and obliterative phlebitis. Which is the most appropriate diagnosis?
choices: A. IgG4-related disease, an entity explicitly listed on the Sjögren's clinical differential diagnosis
B. Primary Sjögren's disease with secondary plasma cell expansion in glandular tissue and fibrosis
C. MALT lymphoma arising on a background of long-standing autoimmune sialadenitis with B-cell hyperplasia
D. Sarcoidosis with parotid involvement (Heerfordt syndrome) and uveoparotid fever in late stages
E. Benign lymphoepithelial sialadenitis from a prior viral infection of the salivary gland tissue
explanation: IgG4-related disease classically features storiform fibrosis + IgG4+ plasma cell infiltrate + obliterative phlebitis + elevated serum IgG4. It mimics Sjögren's clinically (sicca, gland enlargement) and is explicitly listed on the Sjögren's differential.

wrongExplanations.1: Primary Sjögren's biopsy shows focal lymphocytic sialadenitis, NOT storiform fibrosis or IgG4-rich plasma cells.
wrongExplanations.2: MALT lymphoma is a complication of Sjögren's but is a monoclonal B cell proliferation, not the storiform/IgG4+ pattern.
wrongExplanations.3: Sarcoidosis shows non-caseating granulomas, not storiform fibrosis with IgG4+ plasma cells.
wrongExplanations.4: Benign lymphoepithelial sialadenitis is distinct histologically and lacks IgG4+ plasma cell predominance.

eli5: IgG4-related disease looks a lot like Sjögren's on the outside (dry mouth, big glands), but the biopsy is totally different — full of one type of plasma cell and a swirly scar pattern.

stem: A patient develops sicca symptoms 6 months after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The most likely diagnosis is:
choices: A. Drug-induced sicca syndrome from cyclophosphamide preconditioning regimen exposure with chronic effects
B. Primary Sjögren's disease unmasked by the immunologic perturbation of the allogeneic transplant procedure
C. IgG4-related disease as a paraneoplastic phenomenon from the underlying hematologic malignancy treated
D. MALT lymphoma developing rapidly post-transplant from donor B-cell expansion in glandular tissue
E. Chronic graft-versus-host disease, which is listed on the Sjögren's clinical differential diagnosis
explanation: Chronic GVHD after allogeneic HSCT can produce a sicca syndrome that mimics Sjögren's → donor T cells attack host exocrine glands. GVHD is explicitly listed on the Sjögren's differential. Timing post-transplant is the key clinical clue.

wrongExplanations.1: Drug-related sicca occurs but cGVHD is the dominant explanation in the post-transplant setting at 6 months.
wrongExplanations.2: True primary Sjögren's would not de novo emerge in this transplant timeline; the diagnosis to consider is cGVHD.
wrongExplanations.3: IgG4-related disease is unrelated to allogeneic transplant; histology and IgG4 levels would be needed.
wrongExplanations.4: MALT lymphoma typically arises on long-standing autoimmune sialadenitis, not 6 months post-HSCT.

eli5: After a bone marrow transplant from a donor, the donor's immune cells can attack the patient's tear and spit glands. That's chronic graft-versus-host disease, and it can look just like Sjögren's.

stem: Anti-Ro52 in Sjögren's disease targets a protein with what cellular function?
choices: A. Stabilization of newly synthesized RNA transcripts in the nucleoplasm broadly during cellular stress
B. Clearance of defective RNA transcripts within the cell nucleus during cellular stress responses
C. E3 ubiquitin ligase activity in the cytoplasm, tagging substrates for proteasomal degradation
D. Catalysis of pre-mRNA splicing within the spliceosome on intronic boundary recognition sites
E. Stabilization of nuclear pore complexes during interphase across diverse stress conditions
explanation: Ro52 = cytoplasmic E3 ubiquitin ligase → tags substrate proteins with ubiquitin → marks them for proteasomal degradation. Distinct from Ro60, which is nuclear and clears defective RNA transcripts.

wrongExplanations.1: RNA transcript stabilization is not the function of Ro52. Ro60 (nuclear) does RNA quality control.
wrongExplanations.2: Clearing defective RNA transcripts in the nucleus = Ro60, not Ro52.
wrongExplanations.3: Pre-mRNA splicing is performed by snRNPs (anti-Sm targets in SLE), not Ro52.
wrongExplanations.4: Nuclear pore complex stabilization is not a function of Ro52.

eli5: Ro52 lives in the cytoplasm and acts like a janitor — it sticks little 'trash' tags (ubiquitin) on broken proteins so the cell's recycler can chew them up.

stem: What is considered the most likely environmental trigger initiating Sjögren's disease in genetically susceptible individuals?
choices: A. Chronic exposure to UV radiation, causing cumulative cytokeratin damage in the salivary epithelium
B. Viral infection — most likely the environmental trigger in a genetically susceptible host
C. Recurrent bacterial sialadenitis with subsequent transition to chronic autoimmune inflammation
D. Chronic mercury exposure leading to delayed mucosal antigen unmasking and gland damage
E. Long-term silica inhalation from occupational dust with secondary lymph node involvement broadly
explanation: Sjögren's pathogenesis is described as a multistep process triggered by an environmental factor — most likely viral — in a genetically susceptible host (strong MHC association). The viral infection activates type I IFN signaling, which then activates salivary epithelial cells.

wrongExplanations.1: UV radiation is implicated in cutaneous lupus, not Sjögren's pathogenesis.
wrongExplanations.2: Recurrent bacterial sialadenitis can cause chronic gland damage but is not the slide's named environmental trigger.
wrongExplanations.3: Mercury exposure is not the named trigger in this lecture.
wrongExplanations.4: Silica is associated with some autoimmune diseases (e.g., systemic sclerosis, RA) but is not the Sjögren's trigger.

eli5: We don't know exactly which virus, but a viral infection in someone with the wrong genes is probably what kicks off Sjögren's.

stem: Which mechanism describes how M1-polarized tumor-associated macrophages exert their anti-tumor effect?
choices: A. Production of VEGF that paradoxically reduces tumor blood supply through receptor downregulation
B. Production of nitric oxide, which directly kills many tumor cells in the local microenvironment
C. Secretion of matrix metalloproteinases that block tumor cell migration through remodeled stroma
D. Release of TGF-β that broadly suppresses tumor cell proliferation in the local microenvironment
E. Secretion of IL-10 that polarizes neighboring lymphocytes into anti-tumor effector phenotypes
explanation: M1 macrophages = classically activated → produce nitric oxide (NO) → directly kill many tumor cells. M2 (alternatively activated) macrophages, in contrast, produce VEGF (pro-angiogenic) and MMPs (pro-metastatic) and are pro-tumor (CD163+).

wrongExplanations.1: VEGF is produced by M2 macrophages and PROMOTES angiogenesis (pro-tumor), not anti-tumor.
wrongExplanations.2: MMPs are M2 products that promote metastasis through stromal remodeling — pro-tumor, not anti-tumor.
wrongExplanations.3: TGF-β is immunosuppressive (secreted by tumors and Tregs), not the M1 effector mechanism.
wrongExplanations.4: IL-10 is immunosuppressive (Treg/M2 product) — opposite of M1 anti-tumor activity.

eli5: M1 macrophages are the killer kind. They squirt nitric oxide gas, which is toxic to tumor cells. M2 macrophages are the helper kind that protect the tumor.

stem: A tumor that initially expressed strong neoantigens has acquired resistance to CTL killing through 'immune editing.' Which molecular change best explains the lost CTL recognition?
choices: A. Upregulation of HER2/neu on the tumor cell surface to enhance proliferative oncogenic signaling further
B. Increased expression of cancer/testis antigens leading to more diverse tumor antigen presentation overall
C. Upregulation of activating ligands for NK cell receptors in the tumor microenvironment broadly
D. Increased PD-L1 expression on the tumor cell surface, blocking CTL function via PD-1 engagement
E. Loss of β2-microglobulin or TAP1/TAP2, leading to consequent loss of MHC class I surface expression
explanation: Immune editing → loss of MHC I surface expression via decreased synthesis or decreased β2-microglobulin/TAP1/TAP2 → tumors lose the ability to present neoantigens on MHC I → CTLs cannot recognize them. Only happens in immunocompetent hosts under selection pressure.

wrongExplanations.1: HER2/neu upregulation drives proliferation but does not explain loss of antigen presentation to CTLs.
wrongExplanations.2: More cancer/testis antigens would IMPROVE recognition, not reduce it.
wrongExplanations.3: Upregulation of NK activating ligands would increase NK susceptibility, not reduce CTL recognition.
wrongExplanations.4: PD-L1 upregulation is an evasion mechanism, but the lecture's specific 'loss of antigen expression' definition refers to MHC I machinery loss (β2-microglobulin, TAP1/TAP2).

eli5: When CTLs find neoantigens, they kill those tumor cells. The cells left behind are the ones that lost the parts needed to make MHC I (like β2-microglobulin). Without MHC I, CTLs can't see them.

stem: Sipuleucel-T is FDA-approved for advanced prostate cancer. Which best describes its mechanism?
choices: A. Autologous DCs incubated with prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) plus GM-CSF, then re-infused
B. Monoclonal antibody against PAP coupled to a radioisotope to deliver targeted radiation to cells
C. CAR-T cell therapy targeting prostate-specific membrane antigen on prostate adenocarcinoma cells
D. DNA vaccine using a lentiviral vector encoding PAP for synthesis and presentation on MHC I
E. Killed whole-cell tumor vaccine derived from autologous prostate tissue mixed with TLR ligands
explanation: Sipuleucel-T = autologous DC-based vaccine. Patient DCs are harvested → incubated ex vivo with prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP) + GM-CSF (immune-stimulating fusion protein) → re-infused into the patient → DCs prime T cells against PAP-expressing prostate cancer.

wrongExplanations.1: Sipuleucel-T is not a radio-conjugated antibody. It is a cellular vaccine.
wrongExplanations.2: Sipuleucel-T is not a CAR-T product. CAR-T is approved for blood cancers, not prostate.
wrongExplanations.3: Sipuleucel-T is a DC vaccine, not a DNA/viral vector vaccine.
wrongExplanations.4: Sipuleucel-T is not a killed whole-cell vaccine; it is a defined antigen (PAP) loaded onto DCs.

eli5: Doctors take some of the patient's own dendritic cells, soak them in a prostate cancer protein with a booster, and put them back in. The dendritic cells then teach T cells to attack the cancer.

stem: A patient develops cytokine release syndrome (CRS) several days after CAR-T cell infusion. Which mechanism best explains this adverse effect?
choices: A. Hypersensitivity reaction to murine epitopes on the CAR construct, mediated by preformed host IgE in serum
B. Infusion reaction triggered by complement activation against engineered T cell surface modifications broadly
C. Tumor lysis syndrome from rapid intravascular destruction of CD19-expressing leukemic cells circulating
D. Massive simultaneous T cell activation producing an intense systemic inflammatory cytokine release storm
E. Bystander macrophage activation by residual lentiviral vector particles in the infused CAR-T product
explanation: CRS pathophysiology: CAR-T cells engage tumor antigen at scale → many T cells are simultaneously activated → massive cytokine release (IL-6, IFN-γ, TNF-α) → systemic inflammatory response, fever, hypotension, organ dysfunction. This is the signature CAR-T toxicity, distinct from checkpoint inhibitor immune-related adverse events.

wrongExplanations.1: Hypersensitivity to CAR construct epitopes is not the dominant mechanism described.
wrongExplanations.2: Complement-mediated infusion reaction is not the slide's described mechanism for CRS.
wrongExplanations.3: Tumor lysis syndrome is a related but distinct entity (electrolyte derangement from cell breakdown), not the CRS mechanism per se.
wrongExplanations.4: Lentiviral vector residue is not the described cause of CRS in the lecture.

eli5: When millions of CAR-T cells go off at the same time, they all dump cytokines into the bloodstream. The patient gets a huge inflammatory storm with fever and low blood pressure.

stem: Some CAR-T cells become unresponsive over time despite initial efficacy. The proposed strategy to overcome this is:
choices: A. Increase the IgV antigen-binding affinity of the CAR construct to improve tumor cell recognition substantially
B. Add a second cytoplasmic costimulatory domain such as 4-1BB to broaden activation signaling further
C. Eliminate PD-1 expression from CAR-T cells before transfer to prevent exhaustion-related dysfunction
D. Combine CAR-T infusion with allogeneic stem cell transplant to expand the donor T cell repertoire
E. Pretreat patients with anti-thymocyte globulin to deplete inhibitory regulatory T cell populations broadly
explanation: Persistently activated CAR-T cells upregulate exhaustion markers like PD-1 → become dysfunctional. Lecture-named strategy: eliminate PD-1 from CAR-T cells before transfer (e.g., gene editing) → prevents exhaustion and preserves long-term cytotoxic activity.

wrongExplanations.1: Affinity tuning is a different optimization; the slide names PD-1 elimination for the dysfunction problem.
wrongExplanations.2: Adding costim domains improves potency but does not address the exhaustion mechanism specifically.
wrongExplanations.3: Allogeneic transplant is not the named CAR-T optimization for exhaustion.
wrongExplanations.4: ATG depletion is not the described strategy in this lecture for CAR-T dysfunction.

eli5: When CAR-T cells get tired (exhausted), they put up a 'PD-1' brake. If you delete PD-1 before putting them in the patient, they can't exhaust as easily.

stem: Tumors can recur after CAR-T therapy through clonal evolution. Which strategy is proposed to address this resistance mechanism?
choices: A. Pretreat with cyclophosphamide and fludarabine to deplete the host endogenous lymphocyte populations broadly
B. Introduce two CARs with different antigen specificities to prevent tumor escape via single-antigen loss
C. Combine CAR-T with checkpoint blockade against PD-1 to enhance overall effector function long-term
D. Infuse memory CAR-T cells repeatedly at fixed intervals to maintain tumor immune surveillance over time
E. Use bispecific T cell engagers concurrently to recruit additional endogenous T cells to the tumor site
explanation: Surviving tumor cells may lose the targeted antigen (clonal evolution) → tumor recurs. Lecture's named solution: introduce 2 CARs with different antigen specificities → tumor must lose BOTH antigens to escape, drastically reducing the probability of clonal escape.

wrongExplanations.1: Lymphodepleting chemo is standard for CAR-T conditioning but does not address clonal antigen loss.
wrongExplanations.2: Adding checkpoint blockade addresses exhaustion, not antigen loss.
wrongExplanations.3: Memory CAR-T persistence helps surveillance but does not solve antigen escape variants.
wrongExplanations.4: BiTEs are an alternative therapy class, not the lecture's named solution to CAR-T antigen escape.

eli5: If your CAR-T cells only know one cancer marker, the cancer can hide by getting rid of it. Two different CARs means the cancer would have to get rid of both to escape — much harder.

stem: Which limitation explains why CAR-T cell therapy has been unsuccessful in most solid tumors?
choices: A. CAR-T constructs cannot transduce T cells from patients with solid epithelial cancers reliably and consistently
B. CAR therapy has only been successful in hematologic (blood) cancers to date in published clinical practice
C. Solid tumors universally lack any tumor-specific surface antigens for CAR design and engineering use
D. The MHC restriction of CAR-T constructs prevents recognition of solid tumor antigens across HLA backgrounds
E. Cytokine release syndrome from CAR-T is uniformly fatal in patients harboring large solid tumor burdens
explanation: Per the lecture, CAR therapy has only been successful in blood (hematologic) cancers. Solid tumors pose multiple barriers: dense stroma, immunosuppressive TME (TGF-β, IL-10, MDSCs, Tregs), and antigen heterogeneity → so far CAR-T has not translated effectively to solid tumor disease.

wrongExplanations.1: T cell transduction is feasible regardless of tumor type; the limitation is biology, not technique.
wrongExplanations.2: Solid tumors do have surface antigens (HER2, mesothelin, etc.); the issue is not absence of targets but the tumor microenvironment and antigen heterogeneity.
wrongExplanations.3: CARs are MHC-INDEPENDENT — they do not require MHC presentation. So MHC restriction is not the issue.
wrongExplanations.4: CRS is a manageable toxicity, not uniformly fatal. CRS does not specifically explain solid tumor failure.

eli5: CAR-T cells work great against blood cancers because the cancer cells are floating around alone. Solid tumors are tougher — they have a fortress of supportive cells around them, so CAR-T hasn't broken through yet.

stem: Which best describes a tumor antigen derived from an oncogenic virus?
choices: A. HPV E6/E7 oncoproteins, which are processed and presented on MHC of cervical carcinoma cells
B. HER2/neu overexpressed on the surface of breast cancer cells across diverse tumor stages
C. Tyrosinase de-repressed in melanoma cells leading to broader tumor antigen presentation profiles
D. MART-1 expressed by melanoma cells and recognized as a tissue-restricted self-antigen by T cells
E. MAGE family proteins de-repressed in many tumors as classic cancer/testis antigens systemwide
explanation: Antigens of oncogenic viruses → viral proteins (e.g., HPV E6/E7) processed and presented on MHC by infected/transformed cells → recognized by adaptive immunity → highly immunogenic because they are inherently foreign. This category is distinct from neoantigens (mutated genes) and overexpressed self-proteins.

wrongExplanations.1: HER2/neu is an example of an OVEREXPRESSED ONCOGENIC PROTEIN (self-antigen overexpressed in tumors) — not a viral antigen.
wrongExplanations.2: Tyrosinase is a TISSUE-SPECIFIC protein in melanocytes, not a viral antigen.
wrongExplanations.3: MART-1 is a melanocyte tissue-specific antigen, not viral-derived.
wrongExplanations.4: MAGE proteins are CANCER/TESTIS antigens (de-repressed self-genes), not viral antigens.

eli5: Some viruses cause cancers. Their viral proteins (like HPV's E6/E7 in cervical cancer) sit on the cancer cells and look totally foreign to the immune system, so they're great targets.

stem: What does the abbreviation 'TILs' refer to in the context of tumor immunology?
choices: A. Tumor-induced lymphangiogenesis sites that promote regional metastasis through lymphatic spread to nodes
B. Tumor-derived inflammatory ligands that engage innate pattern recognition receptors on macrophages
C. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes that have entered the tumor microenvironment from peripheral circulation
D. Tumor-intrinsic ligands recognized by NK cell activating receptors on the tumor cell surface broadly
E. Tissue-induced lymphocyte signaling cascades that maintain peripheral T cell tolerance broadly
explanation: TILs = tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes → lymphocytes that have penetrated the tumor microenvironment. Few TILs (combined with abundant Tregs) is one named reason >50% of patients fail to respond to checkpoint blockade.

wrongExplanations.1: Lymphangiogenesis sites is not what TIL stands for in this lecture.
wrongExplanations.2: Inflammatory ligands engaging PRRs is unrelated to the TIL acronym.
wrongExplanations.3: Tumor-intrinsic NK ligands are activating ligands but are not TILs.
wrongExplanations.4: Tissue-induced lymphocyte signaling is not the meaning of TIL.

eli5: TILs are just immune cells that have made it INSIDE the tumor. Tumors with lots of TILs tend to respond better to immune therapy.

stem: Which is NOT a named reason that >50% of patients fail to respond to checkpoint blockade?
choices: A. Tumors have few somatic mutations and therefore generate few neoantigen-specific T cell clones at baseline
B. Tumors have few tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and an abundance of regulatory T cells in the microenvironment
C. Tumors do not utilize the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway for immune evasion in the patient's particular setting
D. Patients lack an intact thymus to generate de novo tumor-specific naïve T cells during checkpoint therapy
E. Tumors develop resistance through selective growth of variants expressing other inhibitory molecules
explanation: The four named reasons for checkpoint failure are: (1) few somatic mutations → few neoantigens → few responsive clones; (2) few TILs and abundant Tregs; (3) tumor doesn't use PD-1/PD-L1 pathway; (4) resistance via outgrowth of cells expressing OTHER inhibitory molecules. Thymic involution is NOT one of the named reasons.

wrongExplanations.1: Few somatic mutations → few neoantigens IS one of the named four failure mechanisms.
wrongExplanations.2: Few TILs + many Tregs IS the second named failure mechanism.
wrongExplanations.3: Not using the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway IS the third named failure mechanism.
wrongExplanations.4: Outgrowth of cells with other inhibitory molecules IS the fourth named failure mechanism.

eli5: Checkpoint inhibitors don't work for everyone. The lecture lists four reasons: not enough mutations, not enough T cells in the tumor, the tumor doesn't use that brake, or the tumor switches to a different brake.

stem: Tregs suppress T cell responses partly by 'consuming' a key cytokine. Which cytokine, and how does this work?
choices: A. They consume IL-12, which is required for Th1 polarization and macrophage classical activation pathways
B. They consume IL-4, which is required for Th2 polarization and IgE class switching in B cells nearby
C. They consume IL-15, which is required for NK cell development and memory CD8 T cell long-term persistence
D. They consume IL-2 via high-affinity IL-2Rα (CD25), depriving other T cells of this critical growth factor
E. They consume TGF-β, which would otherwise drive induced Treg generation in peripheral tissues broadly
explanation: Tregs express high levels of IL-2Rα (CD25) → IL-2 is critical for T cell growth, survival, and function → Tregs act as an IL-2 'sink,' depriving conventional T cells of IL-2 → reduced proliferation and differentiation of effectors. This is one of three Treg suppression mechanisms (along with removing B7 from APCs and secreting IL-10/TGF-β).

wrongExplanations.1: Tregs do not function as IL-12 consumers in this mechanism.
wrongExplanations.2: IL-4 consumption by Tregs is not the described mechanism.
wrongExplanations.3: IL-15 is involved in NK/memory T cell biology but not the Treg consumption mechanism described.
wrongExplanations.4: TGF-β is PRODUCED by Tregs, not consumed by them.

eli5: Tregs are like greedy kids at a snack table. They have huge straws (CD25) that suck up all the IL-2, so the other T cells don't get any and can't grow.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of TGF-β as described in the autoimmunity lectures?
choices: A. Inhibition of T cell proliferation and effector function broadly across activated subsets in tissues
B. Activation of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells through enhanced perforin and granzyme B expression patterns
C. Stimulation of IgA antibody production by B cells in mucosal compartments through class switching
D. Promotion of tissue repair after local immune and inflammatory reactions have subsided gradually
E. Inhibition of macrophage activation by suppressing classical M1 polarization signals locally
explanation: TGF-β functions per the slides: (1) inhibits T cell proliferation/effector function, (2) inhibits macrophage activation, (3) stimulates IgA production, (4) promotes tissue repair after inflammation subsides. TGF-β does NOT activate CTLs — it is broadly immunosuppressive against effector responses.

wrongExplanations.1: Inhibition of T cell proliferation/effector function IS a TGF-β function — listed.
wrongExplanations.2: Stimulation of IgA production IS a TGF-β function — listed.
wrongExplanations.3: Promotion of tissue repair IS a TGF-β function — listed.
wrongExplanations.4: Inhibition of macrophage activation IS a TGF-β function — listed.

eli5: TGF-β is mostly a peacekeeper. It calms down T cells and macrophages, helps make IgA antibodies for the gut, and helps tissue heal. It does NOT make CTLs more aggressive.

stem: A child with severe inflammatory bowel disease in early infancy is found to have a loss-of-function mutation in IL-10. What is the underlying mechanism?
choices: A. Loss of CTLA-4-mediated inhibition of effector T cells in the intestinal lamina propria broadly throughout the gut
B. Defective Treg generation due to absent FoxP3 expression in CD4+ T cell subsets specifically in mucosa
C. Loss of B-cell receptor editing in gut-associated lymphoid tissue with peripheral B cell escape and clonal expansion
D. Defective Fas-mediated apoptosis of activated effector T cells residing in intestinal mucosal compartments locally
E. Loss of IL-10-mediated inhibition of activated macrophages and DCs in mucosal tissues, especially the gut
explanation: IL-10 inhibits activated macrophages and DCs (suppresses IL-12 and costim/MHC II expression). It is critical for controlling reactions in mucosal tissues, particularly the GI tract. LOF of IL-10 or IL-10R → unrestrained mucosal inflammation → severe early-onset IBD.

wrongExplanations.1: CTLA-4 deficiency is a different mutation; IL-10 LOF specifically loses macrophage/DC suppression.
wrongExplanations.2: FoxP3 mutation = IPEX, with watery diarrhea + T1DM + eczema, not isolated severe IBD.
wrongExplanations.3: BCR editing defects are a B-cell central tolerance issue, not the IL-10 mechanism.
wrongExplanations.4: Fas/FasL defects = ALPS (lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, double-negative T cells), not severe IBD.

eli5: IL-10 is a calming signal that tells gut macrophages to chill out. Without it, the gut immune cells go wild and you get severe inflammatory bowel disease as a baby.

stem: Anergy in T cells results in part from active degradation of TCR signaling components. Which mechanism best describes this?
choices: A. Ubiquitin ligases target the TCR and TCR-associated signaling proteins for proteasomal degradation pathways
B. Caspase-8 activation cleaves TCR-associated kinases via the death-receptor extrinsic pathway broadly
C. Granzyme-mediated cleavage of intracellular TCR signaling proteins during anergic conversion locally in tissues
D. Autophagic degradation of the entire TCR complex through chaperone-mediated lysosomal pathways during stress
E. Endocytosis-driven receptor internalization and recycling without true protein degradation post-engagement
explanation: Anergy mechanism (signal 1 without signal 2) → ubiquitin ligases tag the TCR and TCR-associated signaling proteins → marks them for proteasomal degradation → TCR-induced signal transduction is blocked → no IL-2 → functional unresponsiveness.

wrongExplanations.1: Caspase-8 mediates the EXTRINSIC apoptosis pathway (Fas/FasL), not anergy-related TCR degradation.
wrongExplanations.2: Granzymes are CTL/NK effector molecules, not the mechanism of T cell anergy.
wrongExplanations.3: Chaperone-mediated autophagy is a different protein degradation pathway, not the anergy mechanism described.
wrongExplanations.4: TCR internalization without degradation does not match the slide's described 'targeted for degradation by ubiquitin ligases.'

eli5: When a T cell only gets signal 1 and no signal 2, the cell tags its own TCR for the trash. With the TCR getting chewed up, the cell can't respond anymore — that's anergy.

stem: How does the death-receptor (extrinsic) pathway of peripheral deletion connect to the mitochondrial (intrinsic) pathway?
choices: A. They are entirely independent and never share downstream signaling components in either direction across cell types
B. The mitochondrial pathway activates Fas-FasL via cytochrome c-driven receptor relocalization to the membrane surface
C. Fas-FasL triggers caspase-8 activation, which then engages the mitochondrial intrinsic pathway to amplify apoptotic death
D. The two pathways converge on caspase-1, which then triggers cleavage of GSDMD and lytic pyroptotic cell death broadly
E. The death-receptor pathway requires Bcl-2 inhibition by FasL to permit downstream activation of caspase-3 cleavage activity
explanation: Fas (CD95)–FasL engagement → activates caspase-8 → caspase-8 then engages the mitochondrial (intrinsic) pathway (via Bid → mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization → caspase-9 activation) → DNA fragmentation and apoptotic death. The two pathways are linked, not independent.

wrongExplanations.1: The pathways are not independent — caspase-8 from the death-receptor pathway feeds into the mitochondrial pathway.
wrongExplanations.2: The mitochondrial pathway does not activate Fas-FasL upstream; the flow is the other direction.
wrongExplanations.3: Caspase-1/GSDMD-driven pyroptosis is a separate inflammatory cell death mechanism, not the apoptosis pathway here.
wrongExplanations.4: Bcl-2 inhibition is not a function of FasL; this is a fabricated mechanism not described in the lecture.

eli5: When a T cell gets the Fas death signal, it triggers caspase-8, which then knocks on the mitochondria's door. That switches on the inside-out apoptosis pathway too. Both pathways end with chopped-up DNA and a dead cell.

stem: A patient with hereditary C4 deficiency has SLE-like immune complex disease. What is the underlying mechanism?
choices: A. Defective negative selection in the thymus due to impaired complement-dependent presentation of self-antigens broadly
B. Impaired clearance of circulating immune complexes due to loss of complement-mediated solubilization broadly
C. Loss of complement-mediated lysis of autoreactive B cells in the bone marrow microenvironment routinely
D. Defective central tolerance due to absent C4-driven costimulation on dendritic cells in the thymic medulla broadly
E. Failure of complement-dependent Treg generation in peripheral lymphoid tissue and gut-associated tissue routinely
explanation: C4 (a complement component) → promotes clearing of circulating immune complexes by opsonizing complexes for uptake by complement receptors (e.g., CR1) on phagocytes → C4 deficiency → impaired clearance → complexes deposit in tissues → SLE-like immune complex disease.

wrongExplanations.1: Negative selection is governed by AIRE/TCR–MHC, not complement. C4 is not required for thymic selection.
wrongExplanations.2: Complement does not principally lyse autoreactive B cells in the bone marrow.
wrongExplanations.3: C4-driven costimulation on thymic DCs is not the described mechanism.
wrongExplanations.4: Complement is not required for Treg generation.

eli5: C4 helps the body grab and clean up antibody-antigen clumps. Without C4, those clumps build up and land in places like skin and kidney — looking just like lupus.

stem: Which best describes the difference between cryptic epitopes and sequestered antigens in the altered display of self-antigens?
choices: A. Cryptic epitopes are foreign-derived sequences hidden in self-protein folds across systemic tissues
B. Sequestered antigens are products of mutated host genes whereas cryptic epitopes are products of pathogens broadly
C. Cryptic epitopes are post-translational modifications applied during inflammation to self-proteins
D. Cryptic epitopes are hidden self-determinants exposed by injury; sequestered antigens are physically separated
E. Sequestered antigens are recognized only by NK cells; cryptic epitopes are recognized only by CD8+ CTLs broadly
explanation: In altered display of self-antigens: (1) Neoantigens = newly expressed self-antigens; (2) Cryptic epitopes = self-determinants normally hidden within protein folds, exposed during tissue injury; (3) Sequestered antigens = self-antigens normally physically hidden from the immune system (e.g., behind blood-tissue barriers) and revealed by trauma. Both contribute to autoimmunity but by different mechanisms.

wrongExplanations.1: Cryptic epitopes are self-derived, not foreign-derived. They are hidden self-sequences.
wrongExplanations.2: Both are self-antigens. Sequestered antigens are not products of mutated genes — that describes neoantigens.
wrongExplanations.3: Post-translational modifications in inflammation describe a separate mechanism (e.g., citrullination in RA), not the slide's definition of cryptic epitopes.
wrongExplanations.4: Both can be recognized by adaptive immunity (T cells/B cells), not restricted to NK or CTL alone.

eli5: Cryptic epitopes are like hidden parts of a folded protein — they pop out when the protein gets damaged. Sequestered antigens are stuff your immune system never normally sees, like proteins behind the blood-eye barrier — they only get exposed if something breaks the barrier.

stem: Bystander activation contributes to autoimmunity following infection. Which best describes this mechanism?
choices: A. Infection activates tissue APCs that then activate self-reactive T cells which are not specific for the pathogen
B. Microbial superantigens cross-link TCR Vβ regions to MHC II directly, polyclonally activating diverse T cells
C. Microbial peptide sequences resemble self-peptides leading to cross-reactive antibody and T cell responses broadly
D. Pathogen-derived nucleic acids trigger type I IFN that broadly upregulates costimulatory molecule expression patterns
E. Pathogen-induced apoptosis releases cytoplasmic self-antigens that drive new germinal center reactions over time
explanation: Bystander activation = infection causes activation of tissue APCs (via PRR engagement, cytokines) → these APCs become activated and capable of presenting self-antigens with full costimulation → self-reactive T cells that happen to be present become activated even though they are not pathogen-specific. Distinct from molecular mimicry (cross-reactivity) and superantigens (polyclonal activation).

wrongExplanations.1: Vβ-MHC II cross-linking by superantigens is a different mechanism (e.g., TSST-1 in toxic shock).
wrongExplanations.2: Cross-reactive responses to microbial peptides resembling self = molecular mimicry, not bystander activation.
wrongExplanations.3: Type I IFN-driven costimulator upregulation contributes to inflammation but is not the slide's specific definition of bystander activation.
wrongExplanations.4: Apoptosis-released self-antigens can contribute to epitope spreading but are not the bystander activation definition.

eli5: When you get an infection, the local APCs get fired up to fight the germ. While they're 'on,' they accidentally also activate self-reactive T cells that happen to be nearby — those T cells weren't even specific for the germ.

stem: Which best distinguishes natural Tregs (nTregs) from peripheral Tregs (pTregs)?
choices: A. nTregs are CD4+ FoxP3+ whereas pTregs are CD8+ FoxP3-, with distinct origins and signaling requirements broadly
B. nTregs require IL-2 for development whereas pTregs require IL-15 throughout peripheral tissue maturation pathways
C. nTregs are made in the bone marrow whereas pTregs are made in the spleen during ongoing immune reactions broadly
D. nTregs and pTregs differ only in surface marker density and have no functional or origin distinctions in vivo
E. nTregs originate in the thymus targeting self-antigens; pTregs come from the periphery targeting self or foreign
explanation: nTregs (natural Tregs) = generated in the thymus → primarily directed against self-antigens. pTregs (peripheral Tregs) = generated when naïve CD4+ T cells encounter antigen in the periphery WITHOUT strong innate immunity, in the presence of IL-2, TGF-β, and retinoic acid → may be directed against either self or foreign antigens. Most Tregs overall are nTregs from the thymus.

wrongExplanations.1: Both nTregs and pTregs are CD4+ FoxP3+; they are not distinguished by CD4/CD8 lineage.
wrongExplanations.2: Both depend on IL-2 (high IL-2Rα/CD25). The cytokine difference described is fabricated.
wrongExplanations.3: Tregs are not made in bone marrow. nTregs come from the thymus; pTregs come from peripheral tissues.
wrongExplanations.4: They differ meaningfully — by origin and antigen specificity range — not just marker density.

eli5: nTregs are made in the thymus and are programmed against your own body. pTregs are made later in the periphery and can target anything (your stuff or foreign stuff). Both are CD4+ FoxP3+.

stem: Which feature of dendritic cell maturation status determines whether antigen presentation favors immunity or tolerance?
choices: A. Immature DCs migrate to skin where they trigger Th17 immunity; mature DCs stay in lymph nodes for tolerance broadly
B. Mature DCs constitutively express FoxP3 to induce regulatory T cells throughout the lymph node paracortex routinely
C. Mature DCs express high levels of costimulatory molecules and drive immunity; immature DCs lack costim and favor tolerance
D. Immature DCs always produce IL-12 leading to Th1 immunity, while mature DCs always produce IL-10 leading to tolerance broadly
E. Immature DCs express MHC class II while mature DCs lose MHC class II expression entirely after activation through PRR signaling
explanation: Per the lecture's factors favoring immunity vs tolerance: mature DCs (fully activated by PAMPs/adjuvants) express high costimulatory molecules (B7) → drive immunity. Immature DCs lack adequate costimulation → presenting antigen to T cells without signal 2 → tolerance/anergy. This is why adjuvants are critical for vaccine immunogenicity.

wrongExplanations.1: The migration patterns and Th17 association described are not how the lecture frames the immunity/tolerance distinction.
wrongExplanations.2: FoxP3 is a TREG transcription factor; DCs do not express FoxP3 to induce Tregs.
wrongExplanations.3: Cytokine output is variable; the named distinction is costimulator expression and DC maturation state.
wrongExplanations.4: Both DC states express MHC II; mature DCs have more, not less, MHC II than immature DCs.

eli5: If a dendritic cell has been switched on (mature), it has lots of 'go' signals on its surface. If it shows antigen to T cells, the T cells attack. If the DC is half-asleep (immature), no 'go' signal — and the T cells just shut down or become tolerant.
